--- title: "Project Title" subtitle: "INFO 526 - Summer 2025 - Final Project" author: - name: "Yashi Mi & Nathan Herling" affiliations: - name: "School of Information, University of Arizona" description: "Project description" format: html: code-tools: true code-overflow: wrap code-line-numbers: true embed-resources: true css: slide_styles.css code-fold: true # <-- add this line editor: visual execute: warning: false echo: false --- ## Abstract Plumbing insecurity—a critical dimension of water insecurity—refers to households lacking complete indoor plumbing, with significant implications for public health, hygiene, and infrastructure equity. While often taken for granted in developed countries, inadequate access to safe indoor plumbing elevates the risk of waterborne diseases, impedes hygiene, and disproportionately affects vulnerable populations across income levels. Tracking plumbing insecurity helps identify emerging public health risks, guide resource allocation, and inform equitable infrastructure development. This study analyzes U.S. county-level plumbing insecurity using 2022–2023 ACS data, employing bar plots, choropleth maps, and spatial clustering (Getis-Ord G) to detect geographic hotspots and coldspots. Using a Queen contiguity method with a 20 km snap distance and a Z-score threshold of 1.96, we analyzed 673 counties for spatial clustering. Results identified hotspot clusters of worsening conditions primarily in New Jersey, Louisiana, and Michigan, while coldspot clusters showing improvement were most concentrated in Virginia and Ohio. Persistent regional disparities remain, with plumbing insecurity concentrated in Arizona and New Mexico—especially Apache, McKinley, and Navajo counties—as well as notable insecurity in Alaska’s Fairbanks North Star and Matanuska-Susitna counties, highlighting ongoing infrastructural challenges and the need for targeted policy interventions. ## Question 1: ::: scientific-box Top counties had the highest plumbing insecurity in 2022 and 2023? ::: ### Introduction
These two datasets provide information on the lack of complete indoor plumbing across U.S. counties in 2022 and 2023. The 2022 dataset includes data from 848 counties, while the 2023 dataset covers 854 counties, reflecting increased reporting in 2023. Each dataset contains seven variables: county ID (geoid), county name, geographic boundaries (geometry), year, total population, number of households lacking plumbing, and the percent lacking plumbing. This analysis focuses on identifying the top counties with the highest plumbing insecurity in each year and examining the geographic distribution of these counties to understand regional patterns of indoor plumbing leakage in the United States.
### Approach
We will identify and visualize the U.S. counties with the highest levels of plumbing insecurity in 2022 and 2023. We first cleaned the data using the dplyr package by sorting counties in descending order of percent lacking plumbing and selecting the top 10 counties. We then created a new variable to classify counties as having greater than 1% or less than 1% plumbing insecurity for color coding in plots. For visualization, we used ggplot2 to create bar graphs displaying the top 10 counties with the highest plumbing insecurity percentages in 2022 and 2023, colored by insecurity level. To visualize the geographic distribution, we loaded a U.S. county shapefile using the tigris package (the geometry information in the datasets were stored as character class strings rather than usable spatial geometry objects), merged it with our top 10 data by county geoid, and created a choropleth map.

Both the 2022 and 2023 maps show that Arizona and New Mexico counties dominate the highest plumbing insecurity group (\>1%), suggesting persistent disparities in plumbing access across the Southwest. Among these two states, Apache County (Arizona), McKinley County (New Mexico), and Navajo County (Arizona) consistently ranked among the top four counties with the highest plumbing insecurity in both years, indicating enduring infrastructure and access challenges in these regions. Additionally, Alaska counties, including Fairbanks North Star Borough and Matanuska-Susitna Borough, consistently appeared with notable insecurity levels, highlighting infrastructure limitations in remote areas. Overall, plumbing insecurity in the U.S. remains concentrated in specific Southwestern and Alaskan counties, reflecting long-standing infrastructural inequities in these regions.
## Question 2: ::: scientific-box How did the plumbing insecurity change from 2022 to 2023 across U.S. counties, and where do significant spatial clusters (hotspots and coldspots) of worsening or improving plumbing access exist? ::: ### Introduction This analysis examines how plumbing insecurity has changed across U.S. counties between 2022 and 2023. Plumbing insecurity is defined as the percentage of households lacking complete indoor plumbing, a key indicator of basic water access. Using data from the American Community Survey (ACS), we aim to measure the year-over-year change in plumbing access and determine whether there are spatial clusters—groups of neighboring counties—that have significantly improved (coldspots) or worsened (hotspots). The 2022 dataset includes 848 counties, while the 2023 dataset includes 854 counties. For this analysis, we restrict the data to counties that are present in both years and have no missing values for the percent_lacking_plumbing variable, allowing for a valid and consistent change calculation. ### Approach We cleaned and filtered the 2022 and 2023 datasets using the dplyr package to remove rows with missing percent_lacking_plumbing values and retained only counties with data available in both years. We then computed a new variable: plumbing_change, calculated as the 2023 percentage minus the 2022 percentage. This measure captures whether plumbing access improved (negative change) or worsened (positive change) from year to year. To detect spatial patterns in these changes, we performed Local Getis-Ord G analysis\* using the spdep package. This statistical method identifies local clusters of high or low values within a geographic neighborhood, helping us evaluate whether counties with similar changes in plumbing access are geographically grouped. We defined a spatial weights matrix based on county adjacency and calculated Local G\* z-scores to identify statistically significant clusters. ::: scientific-box2 Spatial Cluster Classification

Each county was labeled based on the Getis-Ord G\* z-score as follows:

  • Hotspot (significantly worsening): z ≥ 1.96
  • Coldspot (significantly improving): z ≤ -1.96
  • Not significant (no spatial clustering): -1.96 \< z \< 1.96

These classifications were used to identify clusters of counties with statistically meaningful changes in plumbing insecurity between 2022 and 2023.

::: To visualize the spatial clustering, we used the tmap package to create a color-coded choropleth map of the continental U.S., with counties shaded by cluster classification. This allowed us to see where plumbing insecurity is improving or deteriorating in a spatially meaningful way. As a secondary strategy (to be used if spatial significance was limited), we planned a backup approach: identifying counties with a relative change of ±10% or more. This allows us to capture substantial shifts even if they are not spatially clustered. ### Analysis ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/label-me-code-block-5-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Summary: Total counties in continental US: 3122 Counties excluded due to missing neighbors: 50 Total counties analyzed: 673 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/label-me-code-block-6-1.png){width=672} ::: :::
